newsitem.title: USA: China's influence in cotton market seen increasing.
newsitem.headline: China's influence in cotton market seen increasing.

text.p: China's influence in the world cotton market will increase and annual price changes will become greater, an executive board member of Rabobank told a cotton conference on Thursday.

"Developments in the world cotton market, like the liberalization of trade and Just-in-Time trading, will eventually lead to a reduction in world stock/demand ratios," Henk Visser, a member of the executive board of Rabobank Nederland, a Netherlands-based bank which specializes in agricultural finance, said.

"Because prices are affected most by changes in stock, the influence of China will increase, with annual price changes becoming greater," Visser told a World Cotton Conference sponsored by Rabobank International and being held in San Francisco.

Visser said world stock/demand ratio for cotton -- excluding China -- was gradually declining from an average of between 0.50 and 0.60 in the 1960s to an average of between 0.30 and 0.40 during the last 10 years.
"This is in line with a general trend; now that governments are no longer actively involved in stock keeping, commercial companies tend to lower stocks in order to reduce costs," Visser said
The situation in China should be considered separately, he said. According to USDA statistics, around 40 percent of world stocks were now to be found in China, he said.
The stock/demand ratio within China was generally very high, ranging between 40 percent and 80 percent of domestic demand or higher, he said.
"Remarkably, however, China continues to import in years with high stocks. This may suggest that not all stocks are available or suitable for the textile industry," he said.

Shifts in Chinese stock/demand ratios were sizeable, he said. The swings between Chinese exports in one year and imports in another could be as large as 15 percent of world trade. "It is clear that such shifts in demand have their influence on world trade," he added.

The Chinese stock/demand ratio alone had contributed nearly 50 percent to world cotton price changes over the last five years and had made the "Chinese factor" more important than the rest of the world, Visser said, adding that this was "quite remarkable for a country that represents only 22 percent of raw cotton consumption."

"In terms of both trade volume and impact on prices, China has become the main swing factor in cotton. Such swings in world prices, however, are also not in China's own interests; when China buys, prices increase, when it sells, prices drop. If China were able to manage its domestic stocks more efficiently, prices would be less volatile and China could itself reap the benefits," Visser said.
